danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 17
paragraphs: Efter at kejseren havde forladt Moskva, fortsatte livet dér i sin sædvanlige gænge, og dets gang var så helt igennem sædvanlig, at det var svært at huske de seneste dages patriotiske begejstring og iver, svært at tro, at Rusland virkelig var i fare, og at medlemmerne af Den Engelske Klub også var fædrelandets sønner, parate til at ofre alt for det. Det eneste, der mindede om den patriotiske glød, alle havde lagt for dagen under kejserens ophold, var opfordringen til bidrag af mænd og penge, en nødvendighed, der, så snart løfterne var afgivet, antog en lovmæssig, officiel form og blev uundgåelig.

Efterhånden som fjenden nærmede sig Moskva, blev moskvitternes syn på deres situation ikke mere alvorligt, men tværtimod endnu mere letfærdigt, sådan som det altid sker med mennesker, der ser en stor fare nærme sig. Når faren truer, er der altid to stemmer, der taler med lige stor kraft i menneskesjælen: den ene siger meget fornuftigt, at man bør overveje farens art og midlerne til at undslippe den; den anden, endnu mere fornuftigt, siger, at det er for nedslående og smertefuldt at tænke på faren, da det ikke står i menneskets magt at forudse alt og afværge begivenhedernes almindelige gang, og at det derfor er bedre at lukke øjnene for det smertelige, til det kommer, og tænke på det behagelige. I ensomhed lytter et menneske som regel til den første stemme, men i selskab til den anden. Sådan var det nu med Moskvas indbyggere. Det var længe siden, folk havde været så muntre i Moskva som det år.

Rostoptjins proklamationer, prydet med træsnit af en drikkebule, en krovært og en moskvaborger ved navn Karpusjka Tjigirin — »der, efter at have været militsmand og efter at have drukket lidt for meget på kroen, hørte, at Napoleon ville komme til Moskva, blev rasende, skældte franskmændene ud i de groveste vendinger, kom ud fra drikkeboden og begyndte under ørnetegnet at tale til den forsamlede mængde« — blev læst og drøftet sammen med det sidste af Vasilij Lvovitj Pusjkins verssmederier.

I hjørnerummet i Klubben samledes medlemmerne for at læse disse proklamationer, og nogle kunne lide den måde, Karpusjka hånede franskmændene på: »De bliver oppustede af russisk kål, sprænges af vores boghvedegrød og kvæles i kålsuppe. De er alle dværge, og én bondekone kan kaste tre af dem med en høtyv.« Andre brød sig ikke om den tone og kaldte det dumt og vulgært. Det sagdes, at Rostoptjin havde udvist alle franskmænd og endda alle udlændinge fra Moskva, og at der blandt dem havde været spioner og agenter for Napoleon; men dette blev hovedsagelig fortalt for at introducere Rostoptjins vittige bemærkning ved den lejlighed. Udlændingene blev sendt til Nizjnij med båd, og Rostoptjin havde sagt til dem på fransk: »Rentrez en vous-mêmes; entrez dans la barque, et n'en faites pas une barque de Charon.« * Man talte om, at alle regeringskontorer allerede var fjernet fra Moskva, og til dette føjedes Sjinsjins vittighed — at alene af den grund burde Moskva være Napoleon taknemmelig. Det sagdes, at Mamonovs regiment ville koste ham otte hundrede tusind rubler, og at Bezukhov (Pierre) havde brugt endnu mere på sit, men at det bedste ved Bezukhovs handling var, at han selv ville iføre sig uniform og ride i spidsen for sit regiment uden at forlange betaling for forestillingen.
* »Gå i jer selv; stig om bord i båden og gør den ikke til en Karons båd.«
»Du skåner ingen,« sagde Julie Drubetskaja, mens hun samlede og pressede et bundt af trevlet charpi sammen med sine tynde, beringede fingre.
Julie forberedte sig på at forlade Moskva næste dag og holdt en afskedssoirée.
»Bezukhov er latterlig, men han er så venlig og godmodig. Hvad er fornøjelsen ved at være så spydig?«
»Bøde!« råbte en ung mand i militsuniform, som Julie kaldte »mon chevalier«, og som skulle rejse med hende til Nizjnij.
I Julies kreds, som i mange andre kredse i Moskva, var man blevet enige om kun at tale russisk, og den, der fortalte sig og talte fransk, måtte betale en bøde til Komitéen for Frivillige Bidrag.
»Endnu en bøde for en gallicisme,« sagde en russisk forfatter, der var til stede. »'Hvad er fornøjelsen ved at være' er ikke russisk!«
»Du skåner ingen,« fortsatte Julie henvendt til den unge mand uden at agte på forfatterens bemærkning.

»For 'spydig' er jeg skyldig og vil betale, og jeg er rede til at betale igen for fornøjelsen af at sige Dem sandheden. For gallicismer vil jeg ikke stå til ansvar,« bemærkede hun henvendt til forfatteren: »Jeg har hverken pengene eller tiden, som fyrst Galitsyn, til at ansætte en lærer i russisk!«

»Nå, dér er han!« tilføjede hun. »Quand on... Nej, nej,« sagde hun til militsofficeren, »den tager du mig ikke i. Tal om solen, og du ser dens stråler!« og hun smilede elskværdigt til Pierre. »Vi talte netop om Dem,« sagde hun med den lethed i at lyve, der var en selskabskvinde naturlig. »Vi sagde, at Deres regiment bestemt ville blive bedre end Mamonovs.«
»Åh, tal mig ikke om mit regiment,« svarede Pierre, kyssede sin værtindes hånd og tog plads ved hendes side. »Jeg er så træt af det.«
»De vil selvfølgelig selv kommandere det?« sagde Julie og sendte et skarpt, sarkastisk blik mod militsofficeren.

Denne havde i Pierres nærvær holdt op med at være spydig, og hans ansigt udtrykte forvirring over, hvad Julies smil kunne betyde. Trods sin åndsfraværelse og godmodighed lagde Pierres personlighed øjeblikkeligt en dæmper på ethvert forsøg på at gøre nar af ham i hans påhør.

»Nej,« sagde Pierre med et leende blik ned ad sin store, tunge krop. »Jeg ville være et alt for godt mål for franskmændene, og desuden er jeg bange for, at jeg næppe ville kunne klatre op på en hest.«
Blandt dem, som Julies gæster tilfældigvis faldt i snak om, var familien Rostov.

»Jeg hører, at deres forhold er meget slette,« sagde Julie. »Og han er så ufornuftig, greven altså. Razumovskij-familien ville købe hans hus og hans gods nær Moskva, men det trækker ud og ud. Han forlanger for meget.«
»Nej, jeg tror, salget vil gå igennem om få dage,« sagde nogen. »Selvom det er vanvid at købe noget i Moskva lige nu.«
»Hvorfor?« spurgte Julie. »Tror De, Moskva er i fare?«
»Hvorfor rejser De så?«
»Jeg? Sikke et spørgsmål! Jeg rejser, fordi... ja, fordi alle rejser; og desuden — er jeg ikke Jeanne d'Arc eller en amazone.«
»Nå ja, selvfølgelig, selvfølgelig! Giv mig lidt mere lærredsstrimler.«
»Hvis han klarer forretningerne rigtigt, kan han betale al sin gæld,« sagde militsofficeren om Rostov.

»En venlig gammel mand, men ikke meget bevendt. Og hvorfor bliver de ved med at være i Moskva? De ville for længst have taget ud på landet. Natalja er helt rask igen nu, ikke?« spurgte Julie Pierre med et vidende smil.

»De venter på deres yngste søn,« svarede Pierre. »Han meldte sig til Oblonskijs kosakker og tog til Belaja Tserkov, hvor regimentet bliver dannet. Men nu er han blevet overført til mit regiment, og de venter ham hver dag. Greven ville have rejst for længst, men grevinden vil for intet i verden forlade Moskva, før hendes søn vender tilbage.«
»Jeg mødte dem i forgårs hos Arkharoverne. Natalja har genvundet sit udseende og er mere munter. Hun sang en sang. Hvor let nogle mennesker overvinder alting!«
»Overvinder hvad?« spurgte Pierre og så misfornøjet ud.
Julie smilede.
»Véd De, greve, sådanne riddere som Dem finder man kun i Madame de Souzas romaner.«
»Hvilke riddere? Hvad mener De?« spurgte Pierre rødmende.
»Åh, kære greve! C'est la fable de tout Moscou. Je vous admire, ma parole d'honneur!« *
* »Det er hele Moskvas samtaleemne. Jeg beundrer Dem, på min ære!«
»Bøde, bøde!« råbte militsofficeren.
»Nå ja, man kan ikke tale — hvor irriterende!«
»Hvad er 'hele Moskvas samtaleemne'?« spurgte Pierre vredt og rejste sig.
»Kære greve, De véd det godt!«
»Jeg véd ingenting om det,« sagde Pierre.
»Jeg véd, at De var på venskabelig fod med Natalja, og derfor... men jeg var altid mere fortrolig med Vera — den kære Vera.«

»Nej, frue!« fortsatte Pierre i en misfornøjet tone, »jeg har på ingen måde påtaget mig rollen som Natalja Rostovas ridder, og jeg har ikke været i deres hus i næsten en måned. Men jeg kan ikke forstå den grusomhed...«

»Qui s'excuse s'accuse,« * sagde Julie smilende og viftede triumferende med charpiet, og for at beholde det sidste ord skiftede hun hurtigt emne. »Ved De, hvad jeg hørte i dag? Den stakkels Marja Bolkonskaja ankom til Moskva i går. Vidste De, at hun har mistet sin far?«
* »Den, der undskylder sig, anklager sig selv.«
»Virkelig? Hvor er hun? Jeg ville meget gerne besøge hende,« sagde Pierre.
»Jeg tilbragte aftenens hos hende i går. Hun tager til deres gods nær Moskva enten i dag eller i morgen tidlig sammen med sin nevø.«
»Nå, og hvordan har hun det?« spurgte Pierre.

»Det går hende vel, men hun er bedrøvet. Men véd De, hvem der reddede hende? Det er en hel romance. Nikolaj Rostov! Hun var omringet, de ville slå hende ihjel og havde såret nogle af hendes folk. Han styrtede ind og reddede hende....«
»Endnu en romance,« sagde militsofficeren. »Hele denne almene flugt er sandelig arrangeret for at få alle gamle jomfruer gift. Catiche er én, og fyrstinde Bolkonskaja en anden.«
»Véd De, hvad jeg virkelig tror — at hun er un petit peu amoureuse du jeune homme.« *
* »En lille smule forelsket i den unge mand.«
»Bøde, bøde, bøde!«
»Men hvordan skulle man sige det på russisk?«

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: After the Emperor left Moscow, life flowed on there in its usual course, and that course was so ordinary that it was hard to remember the recent days of patriotic fervor, hard to believe that Russia was really in danger and that the members of the English Club were also sons of the Fatherland, ready to sacrifice everything for it. The one thing that recalled the patriotic enthusiasm everyone had shown during the Emperor's stay was the call for contributions of men and money—a demand that, once the promises had been made, assumed a legal, official form and became unavoidable.

With the enemy's approach to Moscow, the Muscovites' view of their situation did not grow more serious but actually became more frivolous, as always happens with people who see a great danger approaching. At the approach of danger, two voices always speak with equal power in the human soul: one very reasonably tells a person to consider the nature of the danger and the means of escaping it; the other, still more reasonably, says that it is too depressing and painful to think about the danger since it is not in our power to foresee everything and avert the general course of events, and that it is therefore better to ignore what is painful until it arrives, and to think about what is pleasant. In solitude, a person generally listens to the first voice; in society, to the second. So it was now with the people of Moscow. It had been a long time since people had been as merry in Moscow as that year.

Rostopchin's broadsheets, headed by woodcuts of a tavern, a barkeeper, and a Moscow citizen named Karpushka Chigirin "who—having been a militiaman and having had a bit too much at the pub—heard that Napoleon wanted to come to Moscow, got angry, cursed the French in terrible language, came out of the tavern, and under the sign of the eagle began to address the crowd" were read and discussed, alongside the latest witty verses by Vasili Lvovich Pushkin.

In the Club's corner room, members gathered to read these broadsheets, and some enjoyed the way Karpushka mocked the French, saying: "They'll swell up on Russian cabbage, burst on our buckwheat porridge, and choke on cabbage soup. They're all dwarfs, and one peasant woman could toss three of them with a pitchfork." Others disliked the tone and called it stupid and vulgar. It was said that Rostopchin had expelled all Frenchmen and even all foreigners from Moscow, and that there had been spies and agents of Napoleon among them; but this was mainly told so as to introduce Rostopchin's witty remark on the occasion. The foreigners were deported to Nizhny by boat, and Rostopchin had told them in French: "Look inside yourselves; get into the boat, and don't turn it into the boat of Charon." There was talk of all the government offices having already been moved from Moscow, and to this Shinshin's quip was added—that for that alone, Moscow ought to be grateful to Napoleon. It was said that Mamonov's regiment would cost him eight hundred thousand rubles, and that Bezukhov had spent even more on his, but that the best thing about Bezukhov's gesture was that he himself was going to put on a uniform and ride at the head of his regiment without charging anything for the show.
* "Look inside yourselves; get into the boat, and take care not to make it the boat of Charon."
"You don't spare anyone," said Julie Drubetskaya as she gathered and pressed together a bunch of shredded lint with her thin, ringed fingers.
Julie was preparing to leave Moscow the next day and was hosting a farewell party.
"Bezukhov is ridiculous, but he is so kind and good-natured. What pleasure is there in being so caustic?"
"A forfeit!" cried a young man in militia uniform whom Julie called "my knight" and who was traveling with her to Nizhny.

In Julie's circle, as in many other circles in Moscow, it had been agreed that they would speak nothing but Russian, and anyone who slipped into French would pay a fine to the Committee of Voluntary Contributions.
"Another forfeit for a Gallicism," said a Russian writer who was present. "'What pleasure is there in being' is not Russian!"
"You don't spare anyone," Julie continued to the young man, ignoring the writer's remark.

"For 'caustic'—I'm guilty and I'll pay, and I'm prepared to pay again for the pleasure of telling you the truth. For Gallicisms I won't take responsibility," she said, turning to the writer. "I have neither the money nor the time, like Prince Galitsyn, to hire a tutor to teach me Russian!"

"Ah, here he is!" she added. "When one— No, no," she said to the militia officer, "you won't catch me. Speak of the sun and you see its rays!" and she smiled charmingly at Pierre. "We were just talking about you," she said with the easy dishonesty natural to a society woman. "We were saying your regiment would certainly be better than Mamonov's."
"Oh, don't talk to me about my regiment," replied Pierre, kissing his hostess's hand and taking a seat beside her. "I'm so sick of it."
"You will, of course, command it yourself?" said Julie, directing a sly, sarcastic glance at the militia officer.

The latter, in Pierre's presence, had stopped being sarcastic, and his face expressed confusion about what Julie's smile might mean. Despite his absentmindedness and good nature, Pierre's personality immediately checked any attempt to ridicule him to his face.
"No," said Pierre, with a laughing glance at his large, stout body. "I'd make too easy a target for the French. Besides, I doubt I could even climb onto a horse."
Among the people Julie's guests happened to gossip about were the Rostovs.

"I hear their affairs are in very bad shape," said Julie. "And he is so unreasonable, the count himself, I mean. The Razumovskis wanted to buy his house and his estate near Moscow, but it just drags on and on. He asks too much."
"No, I think the sale will go through in a few days," said someone. "Though it's madness to buy anything in Moscow now."
"Why?" asked Julie. "You don't think Moscow is in danger?"
"Then why are you leaving?"
"Me? What a question! I'm leaving because... well, because everyone is leaving; and besides, I'm not Joan of Arc or an Amazon."
"Well, of course, of course! Let me have some more strips of linen."
"If he manages the business properly, he should be able to pay off all his debts," said the militia officer, speaking of Rostov.

"A kindly old man but not very capable. And why are they staying on so long in Moscow? They meant to leave for the country ages ago. Natalie is quite well again now, isn't she?" Julie asked Pierre with a knowing smile.

"They're waiting for their younger son," Pierre replied. "He joined Obolensky's Cossacks and was sent to Belaya Tserkov where the regiment is being formed. But now they've had him transferred to my regiment and they're expecting him any day. The count wanted to leave long ago, but the countess absolutely won't leave Moscow until her son arrives."
"I saw them the day before yesterday at the Arkharovs'. Natalie has gotten her looks back and is more cheerful. She sang a song. How easily some people get over things!"
"Get over what?" asked Pierre, looking displeased.
Julie smiled.
"You know, Count, knights like you are only found in Madame de Souza's novels."
"What knights? What do you mean?" demanded Pierre, blushing.
"Oh, come, my dear count! It's the talk of all Moscow. I admire you, I truly do!"
* "It's the talk of all Moscow. My word, I admire you!"
"Forfeit, forfeit!" cried the militia officer.
"All right, one can't say anything—how tiresome!"
"What is 'the talk of all Moscow'?" Pierre asked angrily, rising to his feet.
"Come now, Count, you know!"
"I don't know anything about it," said Pierre.
"I know you were friends with Natalie, and so... but I was always closer to Vera—that dear Vera."

"No, madame!" Pierre continued in a tone of displeasure. "I have not taken on the role of Natalie Rostova's knight at all, and haven't visited them for nearly a month. But I cannot understand the cruelty..."

"He who excuses himself, accuses himself," said Julie, smiling and waving the lint triumphantly, and to have the last word she quickly changed the subject. "Do you know what I heard today? Poor Mary Bolkonskaya arrived in Moscow yesterday. Did you know she lost her father?"
* "He who excuses himself, accuses himself."
"Really? Where is she? I would very much like to see her," said Pierre.
"I spent the evening with her yesterday. She's going to their estate near Moscow either today or tomorrow morning, with her nephew."
"Well, how is she?" asked Pierre.

"She's all right, but sad. But do you know who rescued her? It's quite a romance. Nicholas Rostov! She was surrounded, they wanted to kill her and had wounded some of her people. He rushed in and saved her..."
"Another romance," said the militia officer. "Really, this general exodus has been arranged to get all the old maids married off. Catiche is one and Princess Bolkonskaya another."
"Do you know, I actually think she's a tiny bit in love with the young man."
* "A little bit in love with the young man."
"Forfeit, forfeit, forfeit!"
"But how would you say that in Russian?"
